[AI Is Smarter Than Ever. So Where's the Revolution?](https://open.spotify.com/episode/2hKWPn8scqBy45xWWvIDWR),
Plain English with Derek Thompson, 20 October 2026.

Ethan Mollick, whose new book *Co-Existence* is about how AI is changing the
way we learn and work, talks with Derek Thompson. They discuss how AI makes
experts more powerful while automating the junior work that trains them, why
students perform better with AI but learn less, and whether some friction
should be kept.

**We may now need three kinds of gym.** Mollick first raises the idea of a gym
for the brain, and Thompson extends it to three. Each one deliberately puts
back a struggle that modern life has taken away.

1. **A physical gym.** We are no longer hunter-gatherers, so the body no longer
   gets its exercise from daily life.
2. **A social gym.** A practice of going out into the world and being with
   people, so we don't spend all our time on TikTok and social media.
3. **A learning gym.** AI can do nearly everything, and we still need to
   struggle with things in order to learn them.

**Later, Thompson asks Mollick about four kinds of human knowledge: deep
knowledge, broad knowledge, taste and agency.** An AI can have all four, but a
person who has them gets more out of the AI.

1. **Deep knowledge.** Knowing an area well enough to evaluate the AI's output:
   whether it is at the forefront or making mistakes.
2. **Broad knowledge.** Knowing enough range to ask for more. Someone who knows
   a hundred writing styles can point the AI at different authors, artists and
   styles.
3. **Taste.** Choosing what to ask the AI for, and recognizing whether what
   comes back is slop or something real, since the AI will produce a great
   deal of material either way.
4. **Agency.** Exploring things on your own initiative.

Thompson also asks which of the four is most important. I still need to listen to
that part.

The learning gym is the same problem as the deskilling section of
[The Bitter Lesson for Pharmacometricians](../../blog/posts/2026-10-13-bitter-lesson-for-pharmacometricians/index.qmd):
if new pharmacometricians only review AI-built models, they may never build
the intuition that validation depends on.
